analysis.one_liner: Caps overdraft fees at one per month and six per year, and requires banks to justify the fee amounts.
analysis.headline: The Stop Overdraft Profiteering Act of 2018 was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on August 1, 2018 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have limited how many overdraft fees a bank can charge a customer — no more than one in a month and six in a year — and required those fees to be reasonable and tied to the bank's actual costs, with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau writing the detailed rules (S2, S3). It would also stop banks from reporting negative information to credit agencies when a customer pays back an overdraft and its fees as agreed (S2). The bill was introduced by Sen. Cory Booker with one cosponsor, read twice, and referred to the Senate Banking Committee. No committee action, hearing, or vote ever followed, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 (S1, S5).
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who overdraw their accounts, especially repeat overdrafters. The bill's own findings state that high flat overdraft fees placed significant financial burdens on low- and moderate-income account holders (S3). Under the bill, the most a heavy overdrafter could pay would fall from potentially hundreds of dollars a month to a single fee, and fees would have to reflect the bank's cost of funds and other costs rather than a flat penalty (S3).

how_it_helps.text: Caps overdraft coverage fees at no more than one per calendar month and six per calendar year per consumer.
Requires overdraft fees to be reasonable and tied to the financial institution's cost of funds and other costs, instead of a flat penalty fee.
Bars banks from reporting negative information to consumer reporting agencies when a consumer's overdraft amounts and fees are paid under the terms of an overdraft coverage program.
Directs the CFPB to issue final rules, and targets overdraft programs designed to evade the new limits.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other depository institutions that collect overdraft fee revenue. Overdraft fees are a major fee income source for retail banks, and the bill's caps and cost-justification requirement would directly cut that revenue (S2, S3).

drawbacks.text: Banks' standard objection to overdraft caps is that fee income helps cover the cost of honoring overdrafts and funding free checking accounts; caps could lead banks to reduce overdraft coverage, add other account fees, or decline transactions they once paid.

Critics of fee caps also argue that if overdraft coverage becomes less available or less attractive, some consumers may shift to costlier short-term credit such as payday loans — though the bill itself notes overdraft coverage is a form of short-term credit priced at a high flat fee.
The bill gives the CFPB one year of rulemaking authority and broad discretion over fees and program design, which banks could argue adds compliance costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers who overdrew accounts repeatedly, the cap is a large, direct saving — the bill's findings describe heavy flat fees burdening low- and moderate-income households (S3). The cost falls on banks' fee income, and banks might respond with new account fees or less generous coverage. On balance the bill shifted money from a concentrated industry's fee revenue to the households that pay it, but it never advanced far enough for anyone to test those trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote; it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced S. 3343 in the Senate on August 1, 2018, with one cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other depository institutions that collect overdraft fee revenue are better off, because the caps and cost-justification requirements never advanced beyond committee referral. Consumers who pay repeated overdraft fees remain unprotected by this bill at the federal level.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 3343 on August 1, 2018 to cap and limit overdraft fees.

for.name: One Senate cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Added a cosponsorship; the bill drew only one beyond its sponsor.

against.name: Chair Mike Crapo and the Senate Banking Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred took no recorded action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — and the bill died at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Banking industry
against.role: Depository institutions that collect overdraft fee income
against.what_they_did: Overdraft fee caps directly cut a major bank fee-income stream, and banks have consistently opposed overdraft restrictions; no banking-industry position on this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls were ever taken. The only recorded support came from two Democrats (the sponsor and one cosponsor), and no Republican backing is on record; the bill died in a Republican-chaired committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would cap overdraft fees at one per month and six per year and require fees to be tied to banks' actual costs, directly cutting fee income that banks earn largely from customers who overdraw repeatedly (S2, S3). Banks' interest here runs against the households that pay those fees.
